prompt: Going down group 17 from fluorine to iodine, which of these properties DECREASES?

choices.text: The first ionization energy
The boiling point
choices.why: Boiling points rise down the group (85 K for F2 to 457.5 K for I2) because London dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons.

choices.text: The radius of the halide ion
choices.why: Halide ions get larger down the group, from 133 pm for F^− to 220 pm for I^−, as electron shells are added.

choices.text: The density of the element
choices.why: Density increases down the group, along with melting point, boiling point and depth of color.

explanation: Melting points, boiling points, color intensity, halide-ion radius and density all increase from fluorine to iodine. The first ionization energy decreases (1681 kJ/mol for F to 1008.4 kJ/mol for I), because the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and easier to remove. That is also why the heavier halogens form high oxidation states more readily.

prompt: The colors of the halogens come from exciting an electron from the highest occupied π* orbital to the lowest unoccupied σ* orbital. Why does fluorine look pale yellow?

choices.text: Its π*–σ* gap is the largest in the group, so it absorbs high-energy violet light and we see the complementary color
It absorbs yellow light, so yellow is the color we see
choices.why: We see the complementary color of the light absorbed. Iodine is the one that absorbs yellow light, and so it looks violet.

choices.text: Its π*–σ* gap is the smallest in the group, so it absorbs low-energy light
choices.why: The gap decreases F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2, so fluorine has the largest gap and needs the most energy.

choices.text: It emits yellow light when its electrons fall back to the ground state
choices.why: The color of a halogen comes from the light it absorbs, not from light it emits.

explanation: The HOMO–LUMO (π*–σ*) gap decreases in the order F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. Small fluorine holds its outer electrons tightly, so it needs a large excitation energy: it absorbs violet light and appears pale yellow. Iodine needs much less energy, absorbs yellow light, and appears violet.

prompt: At room temperature F2 and Cl2 are gases, Br2 is a liquid and I2 is a solid. What explains this trend?

choices.text: Larger halogen molecules have more electrons and are more polarizable, so London dispersion forces between them are stronger
The X–X covalent bond gets stronger down the group
choices.why: Melting and boiling separate molecules from each other, not atoms within a molecule. Also, the X–X bond energy actually falls from Cl2 (243 kJ/mol) to I2 (151 kJ/mol).

choices.text: The heavier halogen molecules are more polar, so dipole–dipole forces increase
choices.why: All the X2 molecules are nonpolar, because both atoms are identical. Only dispersion forces act between them.

choices.text: Iodine forms hydrogen bonds but fluorine does not
choices.why: X2 molecules contain no hydrogen and cannot hydrogen-bond. The forces between them are London dispersion forces.

explanation: The halogens are nonpolar diatomic molecules, so the forces between molecules are London dispersion forces, which arise from instantaneous and induced dipoles. Going down the group the molecules have more electrons, farther from the nucleus and more easily distorted (more polarizable), so the dispersion forces get stronger, raising melting and boiling points until iodine is a solid.

prompt: Fluorine atoms are very small, yet the F–F bond energy (159 kJ/mol) is much lower than the Cl–Cl bond energy (243 kJ/mol). Why?

choices.text: The F–F bond is so short that the lone pairs on the two atoms repel each other strongly, weakening the bond
Fluorine atoms are so small that the bonding pair is far from both nuclei
choices.why: Small atoms put the bonding pair close to the nuclei, which should make a strong bond. The extra factor in F2 is lone-pair repulsion.

choices.text: The F–F bond is a double bond that is easily broken
choices.why: F2 has a single bond. Its weakness comes from repulsion between the three lone pairs on each fluorine across the very short bond.

choices.text: Fluorine's outer electrons feel a smaller net nuclear charge than chlorine's
choices.why: In every halogen the bonding pair feels a net +7 charge from each nucleus. That factor doesn't distinguish F from Cl.

explanation: A bonding pair close to the nuclei should give a strong bond, so F2 should have the strongest X–X bond. But each fluorine also has three lone pairs, and in the very short F–F bond they are close enough to repel each other strongly. That repulsion offsets much of the attraction and weakens the bond. H–F bonds do not have this problem, because hydrogen has no lone pairs.

prompt: Electron affinity generally becomes less exothermic down group 17, but fluorine's value is less exothermic than chlorine's. How does the section explain this?

choices.text: The incoming electron enters the small fluorine atom's region of very high electron density, and the extra repulsion offsets some of the nuclear attraction
Fluorine's nucleus has a smaller charge than chlorine's, so it attracts the electron less
choices.why: Chlorine has more protons, but in both atoms the incoming electron feels a net charge of about +7. Size and electron repulsion are what differ.

choices.text: The added electron goes into a new shell in fluorine
choices.why: The electron goes into fluorine's partly filled 2p subshell, completing it to 2p^6. No new shell is started.

choices.text: Fluorine is already a negative ion and repels the electron
choices.why: Electron affinity refers to a neutral gaseous atom gaining an electron: X(g) + e^− → X^−(g).

explanation: As size increases, the incoming electron is farther from the nucleus and feels less attraction, so electron affinity falls down the group. Fluorine is the exception because it is so small: its existing electron density is very high, so an incoming electron is strongly repelled. That repulsion lowers its electron affinity below chlorine's.

prompt: Fluorine's electron affinity is less exothermic than chlorine's, yet F2 is a much stronger oxidizing agent in water (E° = 2.87 V vs 1.36 V). According to the section, what are the two main reasons?

choices.text: F^− has a very large hydration enthalpy, and fluorine's atomization energy is unusually low
Fluorine has the most exothermic electron affinity of the halogens
choices.why: It doesn't: fluorine's electron affinity lies between chlorine's and bromine's, so electron affinity alone can't explain the trend.

choices.text: The F–F bond is the strongest halogen–halogen bond
choices.why: The F–F bond is unusually weak (159 kJ/mol). That weakness is what makes the atomization energy low, which helps fluorine.

choices.text: F2 has the lowest first ionization energy of the halogens
choices.why: Fluorine has the highest first ionization energy (1681 kJ/mol), and ionization energy isn't part of forming X^−(aq).

explanation: Forming X^−(aq) from X2 involves atomization, electron gain and hydration. For fluorine the overall change is very negative (−758 kJ/mol vs −587 kJ/mol for Cl), mainly because the small fluoride ion is very strongly hydrated (−504 kJ/mol) and because the weak F–F bond gives a low atomization energy (+79 kJ/mol).

prompt: The overall enthalpy change for ½X2 → X^−(aq) is the sum of the atomization energy, the electron-gain enthalpy and the hydration enthalpy. For fluorine these are +79.08, −333 and −504 kJ/mol; for chlorine they are +121.8, −348 and −361 kJ/mol. How much MORE energy (as a positive number, in kJ/mol) is released in forming F^−(aq) than in forming Cl^−(aq)?
explanation: Fluorine: 79.08 − 333 − 504 = −757.9 ≈ −758 kJ/mol. Chlorine: 121.8 − 348 − 361 = −587.2 ≈ −587 kJ/mol. The difference is 758 − 587 = 171 kJ/mol more released for fluorine. Most of it comes from the hydration term (504 vs 361 kJ/mol), helped by fluorine's lower atomization energy.

prompt: From chlorine to bromine the electron affinity changes by +25 kJ/mol and the hydration enthalpy by +29 kJ/mol; from bromine to iodine the changes are +29 and +42 kJ/mol. Which factor does the section identify as most responsible for the falling oxidizing ability from Cl2 to I2?

choices.text: The less exothermic hydration of the larger halide ions
The decreasing electron affinity of the larger atoms
choices.why: Electron affinity contributes, but it changes less than the hydration enthalpy at each step. Explaining the trend with electron affinity alone is the oversimplified explanation the section criticizes.

choices.text: The increasing atomization energy down the group
choices.why: Atomization energy actually decreases slightly from Cl2 to I2, which on its own would make the overall change more negative.

choices.text: The increasing first ionization energy down the group
choices.why: Ionization energy decreases down the group, and removing electrons from the halogen isn't part of forming X^−(aq).

explanation: Both electron affinity and hydration enthalpy become less favorable down the group, but the hydration enthalpy changes more (+29 and +42 kJ/mol vs +25 and +29 kJ/mol). Larger ions attract water molecules less strongly, so the hydrated halide ion forms less readily and the halogen is a weaker oxidizing agent.

prompt: Chlorine, bromine and iodine reach oxidation states as high as +7, but fluorine shows no positive oxidation states. What is the reason given in the section?

choices.text: Fluorine has a very high first ionization energy and is the most electronegative element
Fluorine has only five valence electrons
choices.why: Fluorine has seven valence electrons (2s^2 2p^5), like every halogen. Five of them are in the 2p subshell.

choices.text: Fluorine's F–F bond is too strong to break
choices.why: The F–F bond is actually weak (159 kJ/mol). Fluorine's lack of positive oxidation states comes from its high ionization energy and electronegativity.

choices.text: Fluorine is a gas, and gases can't have positive oxidation states
choices.why: Physical state doesn't decide oxidation state: chlorine is also a gas and shows +1 to +7.

explanation: Fluorine's IE1 (1681 kJ/mol) is so high, and it is so electronegative, that it is always the atom that takes electrons. It is found only in the −1 state in compounds (and 0 in F2). Cl, Br and I have lower ionization energies and can show +1, +3, +5 and +7, for example in HClO4, IF7 and [IF8]^−.

prompt: The common positive oxidation states of chlorine, bromine and iodine are +1, +3, +5 and +7, all odd numbers. How does the section explain this?

choices.text: Stable molecules have paired electrons, and forming or breaking a covalent bond involves two electrons, so the oxidation state changes in steps of 2
Each oxygen atom added removes exactly one electron from the halogen
choices.why: Each oxygen (oxidation state −2) shifts the halogen's oxidation state by 2, not 1. That is consistent with steps of 2 from an odd starting value.

choices.text: Halogens can lose only an odd number of electrons because they have an odd atomic number
choices.why: The argument is about electron pairing in stable molecules, not atomic number. Bonds form or break two electrons at a time.

choices.text: Even oxidation states would give the halogen a noble-gas configuration, which is avoided
choices.why: Noble-gas configurations are favorable, not avoided. The odd values come from changes in steps of two electrons.

explanation: Odd-numbered groups like group 17 tend to form odd-numbered oxidation states. All stable molecules contain paired electrons (free radicals are much more reactive), and each time a covalent bond is formed or broken two electrons are involved, so the oxidation state changes by 2. For example, I2 + F2 → 2IF gives iodine +1, and IF + F2 → IF3 uses two more electrons to give +3.

prompt: Orthoperiodic acid has the formula H5IO6. Taking hydrogen as +1 and oxygen as −2, what is the oxidation state of iodine?
explanation: The oxidation states must sum to zero: 5(+1) + x + 6(−2) = 0, so x = 12 − 5 = +7. This is iodine's highest common oxidation state, the same as in HIO4 and IF7.

prompt: HCl, HBr and HI are strong acids, but HF is weak. The sum of the H–X bond enthalpy, electron affinity and hydration enthalpy is almost the same for HF (−272 kJ/mol) and HCl (−282 kJ/mol). According to the section's energetic analysis, what are the two main reasons HF is weak?

choices.text: The entropy decreases sharply when HF ionizes, and strong hydrogen bonds between HF and water must be broken
The H–F bond is too strong to break in water
choices.why: The large H–F bond enthalpy (562 kJ/mol) is offset by the large hydration enthalpy of F^−, which is why the totals for HF and HCl are nearly equal.

choices.text: Ionization of HF in water is strongly endothermic
choices.why: The section gives ΔH = −13 kJ/mol for HF(aq) ionizing: smaller than for the others, but still exothermic. The entropy term tips ΔG positive.

choices.text: Fluorine is less electronegative than chlorine
choices.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative element. Electronegativity isn't what makes HF weak.

explanation: When HF reacts with water, the small F^− ion strongly orders the nearby water molecules and H3O^+ ions, so TΔS is −29 kJ/mol (vs −13 for HCl). HF also hydrogen-bonds strongly to water, which costs energy to break. Together these give ΔG = −13 − (−29) = +16 kJ/mol and a small K_a, so HF only partly ionizes.

prompt: For the ionization HX(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O^+(aq) + X^−(aq), ΔG° = −RT ln K_a. If a weak acid has ΔG° = +12.0 kJ/mol at 298 K, what is its K_a? (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))
explanation: ln K_a = −ΔG°/RT = −12000 J/mol ÷ (8.314 J/(mol·K) × 298 K) = −4.843, so K_a = e^(−4.843) = 7.88 × 10^−3. A positive ΔG gives K_a < 1, as for HF (ΔG = +16 kJ/mol, estimated K_a = 1.6 × 10^−3).

prompt: Hydrogen fluoride boils at 293 K, abnormally high for such a small molecule compared with the other hydrogen halides. Why?

choices.text: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds: the very polar H–F bond gives H a large δ+, and fluorine's small, compact lone pairs attract it
HF has the most electrons of the hydrogen halides, so it has the strongest dispersion forces
choices.why: HF has the fewest electrons of the hydrogen halides, so its dispersion forces are the weakest. Hydrogen bonding is what raises its boiling point.

choices.text: The H–F covalent bond is the strongest, so more energy is needed to boil it
choices.why: Boiling separates molecules; it doesn't break the H–F bond inside each molecule.

choices.text: HF is ionic in the liquid, like a salt
choices.why: HF is a molecular, polar covalent compound. Its high boiling point comes from hydrogen bonds between molecules.

explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so the H–F bond is highly polarized. Each fluorine has three lone pairs at the n = 2 level, small and highly charged regions that attract the δ+ hydrogen of a neighboring molecule. The other hydrogen halides don't form hydrogen bonds, because their bonds are less polar and their lone pairs are larger and more diffuse.

prompt: Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium iodide. Which describes what happens?

choices.text: Iodide is oxidized to iodine, and the sulfuric acid is reduced all the way to hydrogen sulfide as the main sulfur product
Only steamy fumes of HI form, with no redox reaction
choices.why: That is what happens with fluoride and chloride, which are too weak as reducing agents to reduce sulfuric acid. Iodide is a strong reducing agent.

choices.text: Iodide reduces the acid only to sulfur dioxide, as bromide does
choices.why: Bromide stops at SO2 (sulfur +4). Iodide is a stronger reducing agent and takes sulfur on to S and then H2S (sulfur −2).

choices.text: The sulfuric acid oxidizes iodide to iodate, IO3^−
choices.why: The iodide is oxidized to I2 (2I^− → I2 + 2e^−), seen as purple vapor and gray solid iodine.

explanation: Iodide is a stronger reducing agent than bromide. It reduces sulfuric acid to SO2, then to sulfur, then to H2S, which is the most abundant product: H2SO4 + 8H^+ + 8I^− → 4I2 + H2S + 4H2O. The iodine appears as purple vapor and dark gray solid, with only a trace of HI fumes.

prompt: Starting from solid sodium halides, the energy needed to turn X^− into the halogen becomes less endothermic from chloride to iodide. From NaCl to NaI the lattice enthalpy falls by 87 kJ/mol, while the energy to remove an electron from X^− falls by only 54 kJ/mol. What does this show?

choices.text: The falling lattice enthalpy, as the ions get larger, matters more than the easier removal of the electron
The easier removal of the electron from larger ions is the main factor
choices.why: That is the 'over-simplified explanation' the section criticizes. Electron removal changes less (54 kJ/mol) than lattice enthalpy (87 kJ/mol).

choices.text: The energy released when halogen atoms form X2 molecules is the main factor
choices.why: That term changes by only about 14 kJ/mol from Cl (−121) to I (−107), much less than the lattice enthalpy.

choices.text: Fluoride is the easiest halide to oxidize because its electron is easiest to remove
choices.why: Although an electron is easier to remove from F^− than from Cl^−, fluoride is the hardest halide to oxidize because of its high lattice enthalpy and the low F–F bond enthalpy.

explanation: The sum of lattice enthalpy, electron-removal energy and the (reverse) atomization energy becomes less endothermic down the group, so the heavier halides are better reducing agents. The biggest change is the lattice enthalpy, which falls because larger ions sit farther apart and attract each other less. Focusing only on electron removal is misleading.

prompt: Which of these mixtures in aqueous solution produces a reaction?

choices.text: Chlorine water added to potassium bromide solution
Bromine water added to sodium chloride solution
choices.why: Bromine is a weaker oxidizing agent than chlorine, so it cannot take electrons from chloride ions.

choices.text: Iodine solution added to potassium bromide solution
choices.why: Iodine is the weakest oxidizing agent of the three and will not oxidize bromide (or chloride) ions.

choices.text: Iodine solution added to sodium chloride solution
choices.why: A halogen can oxidize only the halide ions of halogens below it in the group. Iodine is below chlorine.

explanation: Oxidizing ability decreases down the group, so a halogen higher in the group oxidizes the ions of one lower down: Cl2 + 2Br^− → 2Cl^− + Br2, giving an orange solution. The reverse reactions don't happen, because bromine and iodine cannot take electrons back from chloride ions.

prompt: Why is fluorine left out when comparing how halogens oxidize halide ions in aqueous solution?

choices.text: It is so strong an oxidizing agent that it oxidizes the water itself, giving HF and O2
It is too weak an oxidizing agent to react with any halide ion
choices.why: Fluorine is the strongest oxidizing agent of the halogens (E° = 2.87 V). The problem is that it reacts with water.

choices.text: It is insoluble in water, so it never meets the halide ions
choices.why: Its reactivity, not its solubility, is the issue: fluorine reacts violently with water.

choices.text: It dissolves in water to form hydroxide ions that precipitate the halides
choices.why: Fluorine reacts with water to form HF and O2 (2F2 + 2H2O → 4HF + O2), an acidic product, not hydroxide.

explanation: Fluorine's oxidizing ability is so great that it oxidizes water to oxygen, 2F2 + 2H2O → 4HF + O2, so reactions with it cannot be carried out in aqueous solution. That is also why fluorine must be prepared by electrolysis rather than chemical oxidation.

prompt: A solution acidified with dilute nitric acid gives a very pale cream precipitate with silver nitrate. The precipitate is almost unchanged by dilute ammonia but dissolves in concentrated ammonia. Which ion was present?

choices.text: Bromide, Br^−
Chloride, Cl^−
choices.why: Silver chloride is white and dissolves even in dilute ammonia solution.

choices.text: Iodide, I^−
choices.why: Silver iodide is very pale yellow and does not dissolve in ammonia of any concentration.

choices.text: Fluoride, F^−
choices.why: Silver fluoride is soluble, so fluoride gives no precipitate with silver nitrate.

explanation: AgCl is white and dissolves in dilute ammonia; AgBr is very pale cream and dissolves only in concentrated ammonia; AgI is very pale yellow and is insoluble in ammonia. Ammonia binds Ag^+ as [Ag(NH3)2]^+, lowering [Ag^+]. The less soluble the halide (K_sp falls from AgCl to AgI), the harder this is.

prompt: For a silver halide, K_sp = [Ag^+][X^−]. Silver bromide has K_sp = 7.7 × 10^−13 mol^2 dm^−6. What is the molar solubility of AgBr in pure water, in mol/dm^3?
explanation: Each AgBr that dissolves gives one Ag^+ and one Br^−, so [Ag^+] = [Br^−] = s and K_sp = s^2. s = √(7.7 × 10^−13) = 8.77 × 10^−7 mol/dm^3.

prompt: ClF3 has three bonding pairs and two lone pairs around chlorine. Which describes its structure?

choices.text: T-shaped, with the two lone pairs in equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid
Trigonal planar, with the lone pairs above and below the plane
choices.why: Five electron groups give a trigonal bipyramid arrangement. Lone pairs take equatorial positions, leaving the three F atoms in a T.

choices.text: Trigonal pyramidal, like NH3
choices.why: NH3 has four electron groups. ClF3 has five (3 bonds + 2 lone pairs), and its shape is T-shaped.

choices.text: T-shaped, with the two lone pairs in the axial positions
choices.why: If both lone pairs were axial, the three fluorines would be trigonal planar. In XY3 interhalogens the lone pairs sit in two equatorial positions.

explanation: The interhalogen structures follow VSEPR. For XY3 molecules such as ClF3, BrF3 and IF3 the shape is T-shaped, with two lone pairs in two of the equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid. The data table shows the two kinds of bond: in ClF3, 160 pm (equatorial) and 170 pm (axial).

prompt: The tetrachloroiodate ion, ICl4^−, forms when iodine trichloride reacts with metal chlorides. Using VSEPR electron counting, how many lone pairs are on the central iodine atom?
explanation: Iodine brings 7 valence electrons, each Cl contributes 1 to its bond, and the negative charge adds 1: 7 + 4 + 1 = 12 electrons = 6 pairs. Four pairs are bonding pairs to Cl, leaving 6 − 4 = 2 lone pairs.

prompt: IF7 exists, but all attempts to make BrF7 have failed. Why do AX5 and AX7 interhalogens form with a large central halogen and fluorine?

choices.text: More small, highly electronegative atoms can fit around a larger central atom
Fluorine is the least electronegative halogen, so it is the best central atom
choices.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen and never occupies the central position in an interhalogen.

choices.text: Bromine has fewer valence electrons than iodine
choices.why: Bromine and iodine both have seven valence electrons. The difference is atomic size.

choices.text: IF7 is held together by ionic bonds, which bromine cannot form
choices.why: IF7 is a covalent molecule, a pentagonal bipyramid. Size is what limits how many F atoms fit around the central atom.

explanation: AX5 and AX7 interhalogens are formed by larger, less electronegative atoms with smaller, highly electronegative atoms, because a greater number of small atoms fit around a large one (e.g., BrF5, IF7). IF7 is the only interhalogen in which the larger atom carries seven of the smaller ones; attempts to make BrF7 give BrF5 and F2 instead.

prompt: Liquid bromine trifluoride conducts electricity. What is the reason?

choices.text: It self-ionizes into [BrF2]^+ and [BrF4]^− ions
It contains free bromine atoms that carry the current
choices.why: Neutral atoms don't carry charge. Conduction requires ions, and BrF3 forms [BrF2]^+ and [BrF4]^−.

choices.text: It dissolves into Br^− and F^− ions
choices.why: BrF3 ionizes by transferring a fluoride: 2BrF3 → [BrF2]^+ + [BrF4]^−. It doesn't give Br^− ions.

choices.text: Liquid interhalogens conduct like metals, through delocalized electrons
choices.why: Interhalogens are covalent molecular compounds, not metals. BrF3 conducts because it forms ions.

explanation: Bromine trifluoride is a yellow-green liquid that ionizes to form [BrF2^+] + [BrF4^−], so the liquid conducts. In a similar way, molten I2Cl6 conducts, which may indicate dissociation into ICl2^+ and ICl4^−.

prompt: Iron burns in fluorine, chlorine and bromine vapor to give iron(III) halides. What happens with iodine?

choices.text: A much less vigorous reaction gives iron(II) iodide, FeI2, because iodine can oxidize iron only to +2
Iron(III) iodide forms, as with the other halogens
choices.why: Iodine is the weakest oxidizing agent of the four and stops at iron(II): Fe + I2 → FeI2.

choices.text: No reaction occurs, because iodine is unreactive
choices.why: Hot iron and iodine vapor do react, though much less vigorously, to give gray iron(II) iodide.

choices.text: Iron(II) iodide forms, but only because iodine is a stronger oxidizing agent than chlorine
choices.why: Iodine is the weakest oxidizing agent of the group, which is why it stops at +2.

explanation: Fluorine, chlorine and bromine oxidize iron from 0 to +3 (e.g., 2Fe + 3Br2 → 2FeBr3). Iodine is less reactive and oxidizes iron only to +2: Fe + I2 → FeI2. Likewise, iodine cannot oxidize Fe^2+ ions in solution; instead Fe^3+ oxidizes I^− to I2.

prompt: Chlorine reacts with hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide: 6NaOH + 3Cl2 → 5NaCl + NaClO3 + 3H2O. Why is this called a disproportionation?

choices.text: Chlorine is both reduced (0 to −1 in NaCl) and oxidized (0 to +5 in NaClO3)
Sodium is oxidized while chlorine is reduced
choices.why: Sodium stays +1 throughout. Chlorine is the only element whose oxidation state changes.

choices.text: Chlorine is oxidized to +1 in NaClO3
choices.why: In NaClO3, chlorine is +5: (+1) + x + 3(−2) = 0. The +1 state is found in NaClO, made with cold NaOH.

choices.text: Oxygen is reduced from −2 to 0
choices.why: Oxygen remains −2 in NaOH, NaClO3 and H2O. Only chlorine changes oxidation state.

explanation: In a disproportionation reaction a single substance is both oxidized and reduced. Here chlorine goes from 0 to −1 in NaCl and from 0 to +5 in NaClO3. Since the decrease of 1 must balance the increase of 5, five NaCl form for every NaClO3. With cold dilute NaOH, chlorine gives NaCl and NaClO (+1) instead.

prompt: In excess chlorine, white phosphorus forms phosphorus(V) chloride: P4 + 10Cl2 → 4PCl5. How many moles of Cl2 are needed to convert 0.30 mol of P4 completely to PCl5?
explanation: From the equation, 10 mol Cl2 react per 1 mol P4: 0.30 mol P4 × 10 = 3.0 mol Cl2. (This forms 1.2 mol PCl5.)

prompt: In the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution, hydroxide ions are easier to oxidize than chloride ions, yet the main anode product is chlorine. Why?

choices.text: Far more chloride ions than hydroxide ions arrive at the anode
Chloride ions are easier to oxidize than hydroxide ions
choices.why: The section states the opposite: OH^− is easier to oxidize to O2, which is why the chlorine contains some oxygen.

choices.text: Hydroxide ions are attracted to the cathode instead
choices.why: Both negative ions, Cl^− and OH^−, are attracted to the positive anode.

choices.text: The anode is made of chlorine-releasing material
choices.why: Chlorine comes from oxidizing chloride ions in the solution: 2Cl^− → Cl2 + 2e^−.

explanation: Because the water equilibrium lies well to the left, the hydroxide concentration is tiny compared with the chloride concentration. So the main anode reaction is 2Cl^−(aq) → Cl2(g) + 2e^−, with a little oxygen from 4OH^− → 2H2O + O2 + 4e^−. The oxygen is removed by liquefying the chlorine under pressure. Hydrogen forms at the cathode, leaving sodium hydroxide solution.

prompt: Natural chlorine is about 75% chlorine-35 (atomic mass 34.979) and 25% chlorine-37 (atomic mass 36.966). What average atomic mass does this give?
Astatine-211, made by bombarding bismuth-209 with alpha particles, has a half-life of 7.2 hours. What percentage of a sample of At-211 remains after 21.6 hours?
explanation: 21.6 h ÷ 7.2 h = 3 half-lives. Fraction remaining = (1/2)^3 = 0.125, which is 12.5%.
